"Almost immediately after his conviction, Ross Ulbricht became a cause célèbre for the libertarian/crypto enthusiast/douchebro set. 

Brian Doherty, senior editor of the libertarian magazine Reason, saw Ulbricht’s life sentence as “insanely harsh,” given that he’d committed “crimes that amounted to operating a web site that other people used to sell drugs”—a view widely held by Big Tech. 

This advocacy was self-serving. After all, if the Dread Pirate Roberts could be sent up the river for maintaining a platform for users he’d never met IRL to sell heroin, offer hacking services, or sex-traffic women, the equally-dorky CEOs of Facebook and Twitter might be held responsible for nasty content posted on those sites—and we can’t have that. Free speech!

The crypto community wanted to #FreeRoss. The libertarians wanted to #FreeRoss. Elon Musk wanted to #FreeRoss. JD Vance wanted to #FreeRoss. In his failed presidential campaign, Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. promised to #FreeRoss. So did Donald Trump. 

And free him he did—on the second full day of Trump Redux. “I just called the mother of Ross William Ulbright to let her know,” POTUS wrote on his propaganda network, Truth Social. “The scum that worked to convict him were some of the same lunatics who were involved in the modern day weaponization of government against me.”

One of those “scum” “lunatics” was Preet Bharara, a frequent Trump foil back in the day. As the United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York in 2013, it was Bharara who’d announced the indictment of Ulbricht in Manhattan federal court.

Everything old is new again.

I’m reasonably confident that Trump wouldn’t know Ross Ulbricht if he was watching Moscow hookers piss on him. The reason I say that is because, in the aforementioned Truth Social post, he gave Ross’s name as “Ross Ulbright,” not Ross Ulbricht—closer than Ross Geller, sure, but still not correct.

The question then becomes: Why did Trump feel the need to issue Ulbricht a full presidential pardon on the second full day of his second term?

There are plenty of political reasons, for sure. Freeing Ross was chum for the deep-pocketed Silicon Valley whales who went MAGA; after all, the crypto sector spent a fuck-ton of money to elect Orange Hitler, and this was a low-cost reward. 

The pardon was a victory for Musk and his ilk. It probably made Barron Trump happy. And let’s be fair: next to the other criminals who’ve received pardons from Donald, the Dread Pirate Roberts is Jack Sparrow Shit. Like, he didn’t even buy furs or jewels or pull up in a Lambo! He had roommates!

But there is another angle to this. At the time of his arrest, Ulbricht was sitting on a dragon’s hoard of Bitcoins. As the DOJ revealed in the indictment announcement:

    To date, approximately 173,991 Bitcoins (worth over $150 million at present exchange rates) have been seized in the course of the investigation, including approximately 29,655 Bitcoins recovered from servers used to run the Silk Road website, and approximately 144,336 Bitcoins recovered from computer hardware belonging to ULBRICHT seized upon his arrest. 

On January 15, 2014, the Bitcoins recovered from the Silk Road servers were ordered forfeited in connection with a civil action previously filed in Manhattan federal court on September 30, 2013, seeking the forfeiture of all assets of Silk Road, including its website and all of its Bitcoins, because those assets allegedly were used to facilitate money laundering and constitute property involved in money laundering. 

ULBRICHT has filed a claim in the civil action, asserting that he is the owner of the Bitcoins found on his computer hardware, and contesting the forfeiture of those Bitcoins.

As of this writing, Bitcoin is at $102,897.60. The 173,991 Bitcoins that were worth $150 million in 2013 are now worth [holds iPhone sideways] $17,903,256,321.60. 

That’s real money! But it’s all lost and gone forever. In 2014, the federal government auctioned off the seized Silk Road Bitcoin for—yikes—$334 each. (Where’s DOGE when you need it?)

Ah, but there is a twist! Two federal agents working the case—whose names, swear to God, are Force and Bridges, which sounds like a terrible network TV cop show—wound up breaking bad. 

After retrieving Bitcoin stolen from Ulbricht by yet another Silk Road scumbag, the agents made off with the virtual loot."

text:
Your $99/month outbound stack isn't building pipeline. It’s making your brand indistinguishable from 10,000 other desperate spammers.

Every "modern" GTM engine scrapes the exact same commoditized APIs (Apollo, Clay, ZoomInfo) for the exact same tired triggers:

• "Congrats on the Series A!"
• "Saw you're hiring 3 AEs!"
• "Noticed you use Snowflake!"

When thousands of SaaS companies buy the same public data to fire the same templates, your edge drops to zero.

Worse, public data is notoriously stale:
• The VP changed jobs 2 months ago
• The funding round closed 8 months prior and budget is gone
• The tech stack signal was an abandoned free trial

You cannot build an unfair advantage on data anyone can purchase for under a hundred bucks.

To win in B2B SaaS today, you have to scrape the un-scrapable.

Un-scrapable data is private first-party context that exists nowhere on the public web:
• The internal project that just stalled
• The specific workflow breaking their week
• The board deadline hanging over the VP's head
• The exact reason their current vendor is failing

You can't enrich that from a static table. You can only get it by asking the buyer directly at peak intent:

Lightweight Capture: Run high-value offers that capture warm inbound demand with zero form friction.

Conversation-First Discovery: Engage the lead within 60 seconds over messaging to uncover their 4 Ws (Who, What bottleneck, When timeline, Why now).

Proprietary Activation: Pass that exclusive intelligence into an LLM to generate 100% bespoke emails and custom voice notes mirroring their exact words.

While your competitors pitch an outdated LinkedIn update, you're solving the private operational bottleneck the buyer admitted to five minutes ago.

Stop fighting over commoditized public signals. Capture proprietary context and let un-scrapable data drive your conversion rate.

text:
People like to overcomplicate cold email

They make it seem like you need a degree in computer science or super advanced technical skills to make it work

All I see online is posts about the “optimal GTM tech stack” and it’s usually a massive list of 50+ tools 

To an extent, you do need to be somewhat technical to understand how everything works or if you want to use more complex tools like Clay

So I wouldn’t say it’s simple

But it's a lot simpler than people make it seem

And you can get much better results than you'd think with a straightforward process

There’s essentially 2 types of cold emailers right now:

The people who have an edge in technical abilities who know how to use advanced tools, pull hyper-specific data and build complex workflows

And people who have an edge in marketing/sales knowledge who better understand positioning, creating offers and writing copy

You need at least one of these to make cold email work

But you don't necessarily need to be great at both

I don't consider myself super technical

Over time I've learned how everything works but there are people 10x more technical than I am

That's not my edge 

So if you want to be good at cold email, you need to know what your edge is

If you're technical, lean into that

Build complex workflows that most people can't

If you're not technical, lean into the fundamentals

Get so good at positioning and messaging that your emails convert even without hyper-personalization

Both work

You just need to stop trying to be the best at everything and double-down on your strengths

text:
In a quiet corner of Hangzhou's Lingyin Temple, beneath the shadow of Feilai Peak, an unassuming wooden couplet has stood for over 400 years. It reads: "Quán zì jǐ shí lěng qǐ?" — Since when has the spring run cold? And opposite it: "Fēng cóng hé chù fēi lái?" — From where did the peaks come flying?

Attributed to the Ming dynasty master Dong Qichang, these twelve characters are not landscape description but philosophical provocation. They do not seek meteorological or geological answers. They ask instead about origin, perception, and the moment a thing becomes what it is. The spring was not always cold — when did it become so? The peaks did not always stand here — how did they arrive? A mountain that "flies" defies physics. A spring that chooses its own temperature defies causality. The question is the point.

For four centuries, scholars have knelt before this couplet and offered their own answers in ink, turning the pavilion into a quiet archive of Chinese intellectual history. But this week, something different happened. Dong Ping, a philosophy professor from Zhejiang University and unlikely namesake of the original calligrapher, was invited by Hunan Daily's Couplet Journey column to walk to the Cold Spring Pavilion and speak about what it means.

Instead of lecturing, he said a new couplet in response: "The cold of the spring has no time; do not seek its origin. The peaks came from somewhere; only then do you understand all phenomena return to their source." It is a remarkable reply — but when asked what it meant, Dong Ping said nothing. He smiled, and let silence carry the weight.

That silence may be the most honest reading of the original对联. The first couplet asks not because it expects an answer, but because the act of asking — of standing before something you cannot fully grasp and letting the question sit in your chest — is itself the practice. In a culture obsessed with explanation, with data, with instant resolution, these twelve characters remind us that some questions are meant to be lived inside, not solved. The spring keeps running cold. The peaks keep standing where they landed. And we keep asking — perhaps not to know, but to remain awake.
This version keeps the historical facts but frames them around the tension between answering and contemplating — which is really what the original article was about. Want it shorter for a specific platform?

text:
It appears in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Yevamot 59b, quoting a Mishnah found in Temurah 30a (Mishnah Temurah 6:2). The Hebrew visible in the screenshot says:

“The hire of a dog and the price of a prostitute are permitted [as offerings], as it is stated: ‘both of them’—two, but not four.”

What it means

Deuteronomy 23:19 prohibits bringing two particular kinds of proceeds into the Temple:

“The hire of a prostitute” — an animal given as payment for prostitution.
“The price of a dog” — an animal acquired in exchange for a dog.

The Mishnah then considers the two reversed—or “crossed”—transactions:

“The hire of a dog” — according to the displayed Steinsaltz explanatory translation, an animal connected with arranging intercourse with a dog.
“The price of a prostitute” — an animal exchanged to acquire a prostitute as a maidservant.

Its narrow legal conclusion is that only the two categories expressly prohibited by the biblical verse are disqualified as Temple offerings; the two reversed categories are not included in that particular sacrificial prohibition.

So the passage:

does not authorize bestiality or prostitution;
does not say these acts are morally or legally permissible;
decides only whether an otherwise kosher animal produced by one of these transactions is disqualified from being offered at the Temple.

This distinction is important: “permitted” here means permitted as a sacrifice under this specific rule, not that the underlying conduct is permitted.

The wording and location are independently reproduced in the Steinsaltz Center’s Yevamot 59b⁠ and in Hadran’s presentation of Yevamot 59⁠. The surrounding discussion begins from the biblical prohibition against bringing “the hire of a harlot or the price of a dog” into the Temple.

Verdict: Genuine text and substantially accurate translation.

text:
Roblox should have appeared before the committee & answered lawmakers’ questions directly. The allegations are serious, its written testimony leaves important questions unresolved, & Texans deserved the opportunity to hear company representatives questioned in public. But the language of “stakeholders,” “seats at the table,” & legislative “negotiations” reflects the wrong conception of representative government. The #txlege is not a private bargaining table where invited interests negotiate their share of political influence. Lawmakers do not represent a collection of stakeholders. They represent the people of Texas & remain obligated to evaluate the facts, hear competing perspectives, respect constitutional limits, & pursue sound public policy.

Roblox also did not remain entirely silent. It submitted written testimony addressing the abhorrent Robb Elementary game, its moderation practices, parental controls, age-assurance systems, & cooperation with law enforcement. That submission does not excuse the company’s absence or answer every question, particularly whether it profited from the offending content. But it is inaccurate to suggest Roblox refused all participation or offered no defense.

Declining to appear may diminish the company’s credibility. It does not relieve lawmakers of their duty to consider the evidence, nor should it become a justification for punitive legislation. A company does not surrender its right to petition government, raise constitutional objections, or explain the consequences of proposed legislation because it declined one invitation to testify.

The suggestion that Roblox should now “eat the meal” the Legislature prepares is also troubling. Legislation should not be retaliation for failing to appear before a committee. Its purpose should be to protect Texans through clear, constitutional, & generally applicable laws.
Texas should vigorously pursue predators, exploitation, illegal content, fraud, & deceptive safety claims. It should demand honest answers from Roblox. But anger at one platform must not usher in a government permission system that forces every Texan to submit identification or biometric information before accessing lawful speech.

Hold Roblox accountable for its own conduct. Empower parents with accurate information & meaningful tools. Protect children without replacing parents, restricting lawful expression, or treating legislation as punishment for declining a seat at someone else’s table.

I wrote a lot about the strategy of the East back in March and again in August, and now September has started to test it. 
(I knew it was coming, I talked about it and recommended trade ideas for this scenario)

Moscow and Beijing play for time, they make the diplomatic process itself the product, they use economic pressure to put the West in a position where every move loses, and they wait for the Western crisis they expect after the midterms before they move. 
The test came through the diesel market rather than through a threat, and the diesel squeeze now has 3 sources, because Gulf net diesel exports have fallen to about 390,000 barrels a day, roughly 25% of their pre-war level, Russian product exports have nearly halted while Moscow bans diesel exports until late September, and Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery, a 400,000-barrel-a-day plant that exported more than 200,000 barrels a day of mostly diesel before it was shut on 27 July, was hit again on 7 and 8 September and remains offline. That third source is not an incident but a sequence, because since 20 July the Houthis have dismantled the kingdom's western workaround step by step, first with a declared blockade, then with tanker strikes from 23 July, then with strikes on Jazan and Yanbu from 25 July, then with the seizure of Yemen's Red Sea coast, Mayun and the Hanish islands between 5 and 13 September, and finally with a pumping station hit from Iraqi territory on 10–11 September, so that a route which carried 4.14 million barrels a day through Yanbu in June has been reduced to whatever the American escorts bring through Hormuz, where commodity crossings run at 11–12 a day against about 130 before the war, and the hedge has become the exposure. 

Since diesel is a price that moves an American election, and since diesel and fuel oil ran 52% above a year earlier in the August CPI, the cheapest lever at hand for the White House was the 1 of the 3 sources it could switch off by telephone, its own ally, and on 13 September the president publicly asked Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. 
If Moscow does not reciprocate, and so far it has committed to nothing while Kyiv has accepted only conditionally, then this is the second and most important of the 3 free yields I listed on 25 August, and it arrives in a larger form than a pause for a visiting delegation, because it relieves the pressure point where Ukraine's long-range campaign had visibly reached Russian society, a fuel supply that by Reuters' count covered only 70% of domestic gasoline demand in late August. 
The other elements read the same way. The peace offer is still a demand for self-surrender, since Moscow still wants 4 regions including land it does not hold together with a NATO ban, and brinkmanship has at least 1 documented dividend, because, as one tracker records it, an allied navy stepped back from interdicting the shadow fleet over escalation risk while a Zircon-capable frigate entered the Baltic in August. 

The sentence I reconstructed in August as the payload for Langley, that Russia can hold indefinitely while the West's own bond market breaks first, now looks self-verifying, because the 10-year sits at 5.02% and the 30-year above 5.36%, levels last seen in 2007, partly through the East's flow war and partly through the West's own fiscal and AI-debt arithmetic, and a payload works precisely because it looks true. 
What did not happen is the thinning-out of Russian strikes that I flagged as the sign of reconstitution, because Russia launched 810 drones and 13 missiles in the night of 6–7 September and roughly 2,800 jet-powered drones in August against about 350 in June, so if reconstitution comes it comes from the moratorium on the ground rather than from silence in the air, which is a different sequence with the same direction. 
China's part is what I called winning without fighting, since Beijing funds the stalemate by absorbing discounted Russian and Iranian oil, with seaborne Russian crude deliveries up 62% on a year earlier in August, deepens a dependence that already looks like a raw-material colony, rehearses a blockade with coast-guard patrols east of Taiwan that rose from about 1 to 5.2 official ships a day while military sorties fell 52%, saw its banks spared by the August package against Iran, and had not confirmed its 24 September White House invitation by mid-September, which in Gromyko's grammar means ask for more. 
Washington answers with sequencing across theaters, because it confronts Iran at sea and in the air while squeezing it financially, stabilizes China while munitions inventories that the CBO puts at 5 or more years from rebuilt are replenished, offers Russia an exit with sanctions policy visibly on the table while a stick waits in the House, declines Riyadh's request to bomb the Houthis for the price of oil, and restrains Kyiv for the price of diesel. From this position the derivation is short. 
Both Eastern principals have a reason to defer any threshold decision until 3 November, provided that the result would change what they do and that their reserves and options survive the wait, while Washington cannot cross a threshold without paying for it in oil before its own vote, so on those assumptions neither Moscow nor Tehran nor Washington chooses anything decisive before the election, and the 7 weeks before the vote resolve only by accident or by a hand that is not bound by the American calendar, most plausibly an Israeli one, since Israel votes on 27 October and has been the year's most willing escalator, or a Saudi one, since Riyadh has flown more than 350 sorties over Yemen by the Houthis' count with a defence pact it has not yet invoked, and the next step in the Houthi sequence, the Yanbu terminal or the Suez corridor, would push Bab el-Mandeb toward the full closure that is a threshold in my definition. 

After the vote the strategy branches. 
If the sanctions authority is enacted so that its use becomes credible, and a Democratic House in January would make it more so, Moscow has a reason to lock in a framework before the stick is used, at APEC on 18–19 November or at the G20 in Miami on 14–15 December, whereas if the authority is not enacted or stays in the drawer the process simply continues and the tone hardens, and Tehran has reason to wait into January if a divided Congress will bind the war powers but reason to decide earlier, in either direction, if it will not. 
The physical tests come in the same window, since winter peak demand on Ukraine's grid, which has lost more than 80% of its pre-war generating capacity, and on Europe's storage, which stood at 65% against an 82% seasonal average at the start of September, coincides with a new Congress on 3 January and an Israeli coalition, and that is exactly the cluster the playbook waits for. 
The move, when it comes, will be capacity-bound, which means hybrid and maritime pressure around Kaliningrad rather than a division and the island chain in 2027 rather than this winter, and it will be timed to the Western decay curve breaking rather than to any date on the calendar.

The market has priced this as a repricing of real yields rather than as a war, and that is the correct first step, because the move was concentrated in real yields with breakevens flat and it was global rather than American. 
If energy prices stabilize at a higher level their direct contribution to YoY inflation fades as past increases leave the comparison window, but further shocks and delayed pass-through extend the process, so there is no mechanical spring deadline for easing, and whatever the Fed decides at this meeting the long end remains the instrument that carries the information, while a hold under visible political pressure would open the credibility branch I described after Jackson Hole. That leaves duration risk in two branches, an orderly grind in which volatility sellers are paid and a disorderly long-end move that becomes a volatility event, and the auction tails are the indicator that separates them, while the disorderly branch is also the break the Eastern playbook is waiting for, which is what ties the two halves of this argument together.

**Spine 07:08:04.** Official inquiry X, 11 Sep 2026. Counsel on the Freedom Calendar cut: **56**. Pre-existing **schizoaffective / bipolar** named on the oath intro — that is his medical history, not the injury claim. Worked as a janitor.

Product, exact dose dates, VISP status: **NOT VERIFIED** on this wrap.

**Spine 07:25:57.** Official inquiry X, 11 Sep 2026. Counsel: **22** now, lives in **Saint John**, New Brunswick. **16** at first dose.

**Clock as spoken / as pinned on official X.**
- First dose at 16: uneventful on the official card.
- Second dose required for school life: volleyball, yearbook photography, events, prom, graduate with friends. She corrected the year on the stand to **2021**. Official card pins second dose **22 September**. Mother took her to the clinic the day it became mandatory in New Brunswick. Long line outside.

People feel **gaslit**, not appreciated, unable to speak about the problem. Other diseases are speakable. This one is not.

Organizer / press line on the same wrap: more than **50** witnesses from more than **1,400** applicants. That is the inquiry’s count, not a census this 14-minute reel proves.

The U.S. unseals charges against 5 members of a Russian intelligence network which has arranging murder-for-hire plots in the U.S. and Europe. 

The men remain at large:

- Yuri Khrameev, 63, of Russia, a former Russian intelligence colonel known as “Colonel Yuri”

- Kirill Khrameev, 27, of Russia, an FSB officer and Yuri’s son

- Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, a Cuban national living in Russia

- Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, of Cuba, also known as “Viking”

- Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, of Venezuela

All 5 are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism.

Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro also face conspiracy to commit murder for hire charges.
 Since about 2024, the group targeted Russian dissidents and, more recently, countries seen as aligned with Ukraine.

They allegedly paid or tried to pay people in the United States and elsewhere to surveil targets and carry out killings, and to attack civilian and military infrastructure in Europe.

The two main plots:

- In summer 2026, Suarez and Castro recruited a U.S.-based person to photograph and film sites tied to a prominent U.S.-based Russian dissident, offering $1,000–$1,500 for surveillance and later $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target. 

When the recruit refused to kill the person, they asked if he knew someone who would and mentioned people in Mexico who could do it. 

In 2025, Kirill Khrameev paid a U.S. citizen $200 to photograph a target in Lithuania described as spreading “lies about Russia.” 

Yuri Khrameev then offered $25,000 to kill that person, suggested methods such as a gasoline bottle or a knife, and, after the recruit declined, offered “simpler” jobs such as setting fire to a warehouse or electrical substation to hit countries helping Ukraine. 

Durruthy coordinated travel and logistics for attacks in Prague and in Lithuania.

Officials from the Justice Department and FBI framed the case as a disruption of transnational repression and state-directed violence that reached U.S. soil. 

The FBI’s New York and Washington field offices led the investigation, with help from Homeland Security Investigations and the National Security Division.

text:
The Company Named After a Record

In 2015, a computer science undergraduate at Tsinghua University wrote a song called "Daydream." It contains a line that reads, in retrospect, like a dare: "My company IPO'd… bought a Lamborghini."

The writer was Yang Zhilin, drummer and lyricist of a campus rock band named Splay — after the splay tree, a self-adjusting data structure. He has since said he wrote the lyric as a warning to himself against utilitarianism. In 2025, his company Kimi K2 would be called "another DeepSeek moment" by Nature. In July 2026 it released K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter model and the largest open-weights model ever shipped. This September it confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO, reportedly seeking up to five billion dollars at a valuation near fifty billion. He is thirty-three.

This is the story of Moonshot AI — what the record actually shows, and what two widely repeated myths get wrong.

I. The founder was never an outsider

The lazy version of this story frames Yang Zhilin as a talented nobody who caught a wave. The documented version is different. He won Guangdong's informatics olympiad, scored 667 on the gaokao as Shantou's top science student, and entered Tsinghua — twice moving tracks: from thermal engineering into computer science, reportedly after reading a Haruki Murakami novel that featured a gifted programmer. He graduated first in his grade.

Then CMU's Language Technologies Institute, a PhD in four years under Ruslan Salakhutdinov and William Cohen. Along the way: first author of XLNet, co-first of Transformer-XL — recurrence-based long-context work that predates and underpins the agenda he would later sell. Press aggregates put his citation count above twenty thousand; careful per-index checks land lower, but no honest reading of the list makes him lucky. He interned at Facebook AI Research under Jason Weston and at Google Brain under Quoc Le. He co-founded his first company, Recurrent AI — a sales-conversation-intelligence startup — in 2016, while still a student. It raised about fifty million dollars across two rounds and still operates. He left in 2021, contributed to Huawei's PanGu and BAAI's WuDao large models, took an assistant professorship at Tsinghua, and watched ChatGPT land.

In his own telling, late 2022 was "frustration and excitement." He took a trip to the United States, did the math, and concluded he could raise a hundred million dollars within months — and that the window was weeks wide, not years. "Miss April," he later said of spring 2023, "and there's basically no chance."

The band matters more than the biography does. Splay's lead guitarist, Zhou Xinyu, became a Moonshot co-founder. Its bassist later co-founded SenseTime. A visit to Moonshot's Beijing office today finds a white piano at the entrance and a vinyl copy of Pink Floyd's The Dark Side of the Moon beside it. Every meeting room is named after a rock band — Pink Floyd, the Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin, Queen, Radiohead, Oasis — and one is named Splay, after their own. Candidates are reportedly asked one question early: what's your favorite album?

II. The name is on tape

In March 2023 — fifty years, to the year, after the release of The Dark Side of the Moon — Yang registered 月之暗面, "the dark side of the moon," in Beijing's Haidian district. Asked about the name on tape in a November 2023 GeekPark interview, he didn't launder it into strategy: "It comes from the Pink Floyd album, The Dark Side of the Moon. The founders all love rock music. We used to play in bands. And 2023 happened to be the album's 50th anniversary." Then the line that does the cultural work of a thousand position papers: the album's lead track, "Brain Damage," is about a person experiencing hallucination — "and fifty years later, here we are trying to fix hallucination in large models."

The music is an operating system, not a poster. Subscription tiers are Italian tempo markings — Andante, Moderato, Allegretto, Allegro, Vivace. The company's first agentic product mode, gray-tested in September 2025, was codenamed "OK Computer," after Radiohead. When internal-test Kimi was asked what 月之暗面 should mean, the model offered Pink Floyd — and Kubrick's 2001 monolith; an early investor's fund is literally named Monolith. K2, the flagship line, decodes to 乔戈里峰 — K2, the mountain, the world's hardest climb — per Yang himself: "Climbers face the perilous peak; innovators face the unknown dark side." Even the engineers' slang bends lunar: the serving stack is Mooncake, the moon cake; the night-shift harvesting of idle inference GPUs is called "Tide GPU." When the product named "Kimi" — Yang's own English nickname, on the Splay roster a decade before any company existed — grew too big for the man, the office solved it like a band solving for two members with the same first name: he was internally renamed KK.

III. Two doctrines, two reversals

The founding doctrine, stated plainly in late 2023, had three planks. Context length is the wedge: "Transformer is the new computer; parameter count is its CPU; context length is its memory." Consumer is the loop: only a super-app closes the feedback cycle fast enough. And closed source wins, because owning model evolution is product differentiation.

Moonshot executed on all three immediately. Kimi Chat, announced October 2023, was the world's first assistant to accept roughly two hundred thousand Chinese characters of input — before anyone else shipped anything close. In March 2024 it stretched to two million characters and buckled under a two-day traffic-outage; by month-end it was the second-most-visited chatbot in China. Alibaba led a round above one billion dollars that February — the largest single financing in Chinese LLM history — taking roughly thirty-six percent, partly paid in cloud credits.

Both planks broke. Consumer first: MAU peaked near thirty-six million in late 2024, willingness to pay stayed thin, user-acquisition spend stopped, and the curve sagged. Open source second: DeepSeek's January 2025 run proved that openness builds the ecosystem, the trust, and the standard. Yang's internal verdict, documented later: "DeepSeek saved us."

The reversals were total and self-explained. July 11, 2025: Kimi K2, a 1.04-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts with 32 billion active, trained for 15.5 trillion tokens without a single loss spike, released open-weight under a modified MIT license — no warm-up, literally overnight, per Chinese reporting. It topped the open-model arena and Hugging Face's download charts within days. By 2026, the API accounted for over seventy percent of revenue; ARR ran from roughly a hundred million in March to about three hundred million by June. K2's successors — K2.5 with a hundred coordinating sub-agents, K2.6 with three hundred sub-agents and four-thousand-plus tool calls in demos exceeding thirteen hours, the MIT-licensed Kimi Code command-line tool whose default sub-agent timeout is two hours, on the documented philosophy that sub-agents are workers doing real work, not tool calls that might hang — turned Moonshot into the agentic-coding reference stack. American products now stand on those weights: Cursor's Composer, Cognition's Devin, Thinking Machines' Inkling, Harvey's legal model. On July 16, 2026, K3 launched at the World AI Conference: 2.8 trillion parameters, 104 billion active, a million-token context, novel linear-attention hybrids the field had spent a year reading in Moonshot's own open papers. Downloads hit two million in a month. Demand was heavy enough that the company briefly paused new sign-ups, GPU-maxxed.

Read the speed honestly: a five-person founding team, four from Tsinghua, with a stated doctrine of talent density over headcount and roughly eighty employees at the end of year one — while big tech hoarded compliant chips in six-figure volumes and DeepSeek sat on a pre-ban stockpile.

IV. The Jensen Huang story is not what you heard

Here is the version circulating: Jensen Huang personally vouched for Yang Zhilin, securing Moonshot some twenty thousand NVIDIA GPUs around 2023 — the only Chinese AI startup so blessed. A dedicated mission checked it against English and Chinese reporting, verb by verb. Every component is real. The assembly is false.

The twenty thousand chips exist — as a reported Bloomberg scoop dated July 31, 2026: a computing-power agreement with Alibaba Cloud for the use of "around 20,000" Hopper-generation NVIDIA chips. Sources said "mainly H200" and Alibaba called the H200 detail "completely groundless" — while not denying the agreement itself. It is a lease of Alibaba-owned chips from Moonshot's largest shareholder. It is not from 2023; no source reports any 2023 allocation, and Moonshot's documented early compute was rented ByteDance Volcano Engine clusters plus Alibaba credits. It is not a direct NVIDIA allocation; no source names any NVIDIA role, and NVIDIA declined comment. And it is not unique: DeepSeek, https://t.co/mNc8q0dcNB, MiniMax and every Chinese tech giant command comparable or larger supply — most of it bought, not leased.

The "personally vouched" leg is weaker still. Searches of the exact Chinese verbs for guaranteeing, specially approving, or personally signing off returned zero hits. What actually exists, documented and confirmed: Yang was the only founder of an independent Chinese LLM startup handed a GTC 2026 main-stage keynote slot — 钦点, "hand-picked," in the Chinese press — where Huang name-checked Kimi from the stage. A year earlier at Beijing's Chain Expo, Huang's keynote praised eleven Chinese companies and omitted Moonshot; the next day, in a fireside chat, he added, "and Moonshot's Kimi — they are outstanding." The thinness of that first list suggests a new relationship, not an old patronage. In July 2026, in the K3 news cycle, Huang told Axios "these Chinese models are excellent," called security fears a "misconception," and spent that week in Washington lobbying against restrictions on open-weight models.

One more inversion completes the picture. The White House's own claim about Moonshot's frontier chips — aired by OSTP director Michael Kratsios on July 22, 2026 — is that Moonshot accessed Blackwell-class GB300s via Thailand, an accusation of circumvention under rules Washington had just tightened. The same week the myth says NVIDIA blessed the pipeline, the US government was alleging the pipeline was gray. The causality also runs backward from the myth: Huang's documented attention tracks Kimi's western reception — the Nature headline, the arena rankings, the trillion-token weeks on OpenRouter — it does not create it. The endorsement is of the work, not the supply chain.

V. The rumor that died on the registries

Every research fleet needs a negative result to prove it's working. This one has a good one. Sometime in 2025, a rumor formed that Moonshot had run a stealth model on the public arenas under the codename "ayanokoji" — Kiyotaka Ayanokoji, the protagonist of the light novel and anime Classroom of the Elite: a boy who deliberately scores exactly fifty out of a hundred on every subject, hides an elite ability engineered in a secret facility called the White Room, and quietly orchestrates his class's victories from the shadows while others take the credit. As a stealth-lab persona, it is perfect. That is precisely the problem.

A mission spent itself checking every registry that would have to contain such a model. The census of all fourteen-plus stealth listings ever run on OpenRouter — Quasar was GPT-4.1, Horizon was early GPT-5, Hunter and Healer were Xiaomi, Ox was https://t.co/KFSqx2Jo1a — contains no ayanokoji. LMArena's own deprecated-model list: no match. The academic Leaderboard Illusion scrape that names all fourteen anonymized private arena models: no ayanokoji. A community unlocker tool with one hundred fifty dumped codenames: no. Wayback Machine captures of the LMArena leaderboard across June, July and August 2025 — the alleged window — read model by model: photons, bagels, clownfish, krakens, a velocilux; no ayanokoji at any date. Kimi K2 appears in July 2025 under its own legal name. Chinese media, which documents Moonshot's naming habits obsessively, has never printed the word. The only LLM actually named "ayanokoji" is an unrelated fan-made 27B abliterated Qwen on Featherless, persona-stacked toward erotica, never on any arena. Founder check, trilingual, thirty-plus queries: Yang Zhilin has no documented anime interest whatsoever — his externalized enthusiasms are rock, Murakami, Kubrick, David Deutsch, Steve Jobs, and exactly the naming system above. If anime were in the bloodstream, this is the company where it would show.

The inference left standing: the claim was never a sighting, it was a metaphor that faxed itself into a fact. The character fits a "hidden genius stealth model" so snugly that repeating the fit felt like reporting a finding. The registries disagree, and the registries win.

Moonshot's real stealth practice is quieter and stranger: on LMArena it tests under fruit-flavored homophones of the release names — "Kiwido" before K2.5, "Kiwire" before K2.6, "Kivine" the day before K3 launched — a pattern mapped by the community, never once confirmed by the company, which stays silent on every codename. When a "korrine" appeared on the coding arena in August 2026 and was briefly hailed as a new Kimi, the community rejected it themselves: the tokenizer fingerprinted Qwen, and, more poetically, "Ko-" broke the "Ki-" rule.

VI. What the company actually is

State money is in the cap table now — the National AI Industry Investment Fund anchored July's 3.5-billion-dollar round — and Moonshot answers simultaneously to a Hong Kong IPO filing, a Hangzhou arbitration it never settled, House subpoenas of its American customers, Anthropic's two distillation accusations, a White House chip-circumvention allegation, and an export-control stack that bans in cascade whatever it trained on last. That is not a startup environment; it is an obstacle course on fire. The outfit holding lane position through it sells tempo-marked subscriptions, asks interviewees about albums, and keeps a splay-tree band name on a meeting-room door.

"Those who get it, get it," employees told the Chinese magazine Renwu, asking the writer not to overplay the Pink Floyd angle. The record confirms the angle doesn't need their help: the founder drummed it into the cap table, the code names, the pricing page, and the doorbell. Brain Damage is the lead track. The moon has a far side. The company made both of those into a mission statement and then — this is the part the myths keep missing — the mission statement shipped on schedule.

Report card, for the honest reader: company — confirmed. Founder — confirmed. Album — confirmed, on tape. Jensen's vouch — lore; the record shows a stage, a compliment, and a lobbying trip. Ayanokoji — lore, contradicted by every registry that counts. The one that got away from all of them, the band kid, is documented best of all: he said in 2015 what the company would do, and then it did it.

The postwar US-led order created unusually favorable security, financial, and institutional conditions for international commerce. Those conditions enabled unprecedented globalization and specialization. Declining American dominance does not automatically end globalization, but it can increase security and transaction costs, encourage economic blocs and redundancy, and expose highly concentrated supply-chain dependencies. Where critical inputs lack substitutes, fragmentation can produce nonlinear disruptions rather than merely higher prices.

Modern technological civilization depends on something deeper than individual national ingenuity: an extraordinary international division of labor in which countries, companies, and even individual factories specialize in capabilities that others cannot readily duplicate. Globalization enlarged markets enough to make that extreme specialization economical, helping create technologies whose supply chains now span dozens of countries and contain genuine chokepoints with few short-term substitutes.

It is substantially correct that serious fragmentation would reduce efficiency, disrupt specialization, and potentially slow technological progress. Where pessimistic forecasts go too far, however, is treating those losses as inevitably producing technological regression. Modern civilization retains scientific knowledge, enormous adaptive capacity, alternative designs, redundancy, AI-assisted engineering, and the ability to preserve specialization within allied economic blocs.

The real danger is not deglobalization itself, but the simultaneous loss of several complementary and poorly substitutable capabilities. Under those conditions, failures could interact nonlinearly, overwhelming redundancies that work perfectly well against isolated disruptions. The conceptual formula 𝖳𝖾𝖼𝗁𝗇𝗈𝗅𝗈𝗀𝗒 = 𝖲𝗉𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇 𝗑 𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇 is too simple to be literally true, but as a warning about the networked foundations of modern technological capability, it remains surprisingly strong.

Iran does not need to defeat the United States militarily to impose extraordinary costs on the global system. Its geographic position and network of aligned regional actors give it leverage over some of the world's most important energy and shipping arteries, particularly the Strait of Hormuz and routes connected to the Red Sea.

Events in 2026 have provided a partial real-world test of these vulnerabilities: shipping through Hormuz has fallen dramatically from prewar levels, war-risk and cargo-insurance costs have surged, energy prices have risen, Asian buyers have scrambled for substitutes, and even Saudi Arabia's critical pipeline bypass around Hormuz has itself become a target. This demonstrates a crucial insight: economic disruption does not require physically closing a waterway; making passage sufficiently unpredictable can cause shipowners, insurers, and markets to alter behavior on their own.

Yet the system has also demonstrated substantial resilience through rerouting, fuel substitution, alternative suppliers, inventories, and price signals, while Iran itself has powerful incentives not to destroy an economic system upon which it and its partners depend. The real systemic danger lies not in any single state single-handedly stopping global trade, but in several chokepoints and their backup systems failing simultaneously. Under those conditions, redundancies can become correlated failures, allowing regional military events to propagate nonlinearly into the global economy.

Severe Iranian disruption can place enormous pressure on the United States to respond, but claims that "game theory" ultimately forces Washington to destroy Iranian power and desalination infrastructure go well beyond what game theory or current evidence supports. Strategic interaction offers many intermediate choices, including attacks on military systems, maritime protection, economic pressure, cyber operations, negotiation, and de-escalation, while attacks affecting electricity and especially water infrastructure carry extraordinary humanitarian, legal, diplomatic, and retaliatory consequences.

Importantly, those consequences need not require destroying an entire generating system: because modern electrical grids connect power generation with water pumping, communications, transportation, industry, energy production, and other essential services, disruption of a relatively limited number of important nodes could potentially produce cascading effects far beyond their immediate military purpose. The vital insight is therefore not determinism, but the danger of an escalation trap: one party disrupts commerce, the second attacks military capabilities, the first retaliates more broadly, and target sets expand in response. Each individual decision can appear rational while repeated iterations gradually move both sides toward an outcome neither originally wanted.

Countervailing pressures remain substantial, including strained US munition inventories, competing requirements in Asia and elsewhere, vulnerable Gulf allies, economic costs, and negotiated off-ramps. Deterministic claims overstate the destination but identify a credible mechanism: prolonged conflict continually changes the payoff matrix, while interconnected infrastructure can magnify the consequences of each successive escalation, allowing yesterday's unacceptable action to become tomorrow's seemingly reasonable response.

Models of a cascading resource crisis rest on several strong mechanisms: energy disruption raises fuel and fertilizer costs, reduced agricultural inputs can lower crop yields, and water stress can compound pressure on food production, industry, electricity, and urban life. These systems are interconnected, so simultaneous disruption can produce consequences much larger than any single shortage would suggest.

Linear migration theories, however, oversimplify reality. Food and water insecurity can contribute to displacement, but conflict, poverty, government capacity, employment, and household resources strongly influence whether people move at all, and most forced displacement remains within the affected country or neighboring states rather than flowing directly toward wealthy nations. Migration itself can also function as a circuit breaker by supplying workers to aging economies and generating remittances for vulnerable communities. The more useful variable may therefore be not migration alone, but the rate of arrivals relative to a receiving society's capacity to provide housing, employment, healthcare, education, and integration.

The strongest insight appears at the systems level: a drought, fertilizer shortage, refugee crisis, or energy shock can usually be absorbed individually, but simultaneous crises force supposedly independent safety mechanisms to compete for the same money, infrastructure, commodities, and political attention. The danger lies less in any single shortage causing collapse than in several stresses arriving together and progressively exhausting the buffers designed to contain them.

There is firm ground for arguing that sustained economic shocks, rapid social change, and migration pressures can alter political attitudes, reduce institutional trust, and increase polarization, but leapfrogging directly from political stress to guaranteed civil war moves too quickly. Political outcomes depend heavily on perception, competing narratives, integration capacity, institutional strength, and whether citizens retain trusted peaceful mechanisms for changing policy and government. Migration itself does not push every society in one ideological direction, and successful integration can transform an initial burden on housing and services into workers, taxpayers, entrepreneurs, and demographic resilience.

A stronger political mechanism requires neither authoritarianism nor civil conflict: economic insecurity and geopolitical risk can lead perfectly functioning democracies to favor tighter borders, domestic production, industrial subsidies, tariffs, export controls, and reduced dependence on foreign rivals. Those individually rational choices can collectively reduce globalization, increase costs, and generate further economic insecurity, creating a self-reinforcing loop between fragmentation and political pressure.

As elsewhere in systemic models, institutional resilience acts like spare capacity in an engineered system: the same external shock can be absorbed by one society and destabilize another. Apocalyptic endpoints are far too certain, but the feedback loop connecting economic stress, political response, and further deglobalization is considerably stronger than any single prediction of internal conflict.

Arguing that weakening confidence in the existing international order can produce self-reinforcing security competition rests on strong ground. Governments confronted with uncertainty rationally increase military capability, diversify critical supply chains, restrict sensitive technology, and reduce dependence on potential adversaries; indeed, military spending has risen sharply across Europe and Asia while economic security increasingly shapes trade policy.

Those measures can strengthen deterrence and make countries more resilient, and alliances plus nuclear deterrence remain powerful barriers to direct great-power war. Yet the same adaptations can have unintended effects: economic de-risking reduces interdependence, rearmament creates security dilemmas, alliances couple previously separate regional crises, and sanctions and export controls fragment trade even when kinetic war is successfully avoided. China-Japan dynamics, particularly through a Taiwan contingency, and Russia-Europe friction are genuine escalation pathways without making war between them inevitable.

The core insight survives without specific predictions coming to pass: individually rational efforts to become safer can collectively produce a world that is more heavily armed, less economically interconnected, and increasingly organized into competing blocs. As interdependence falls, one economic restraint on confrontation weakens, while growing geopolitical competition encourages still more self-reliance and fragmentation. The result is another feedback loop in which preparations intended to prevent conflict can gradually erode some of the economic relationships that previously made conflict so costly.

Ultimate predictions of civilizational collapse are not established by the evidence, but the systemic-risk model underneath them survives surprisingly well. Modern civilization is composed of deeply interconnected energy, trade, technological, financial, food, water, infrastructure, and political systems whose redundancies often depend upon one another. A single disruption can usually be absorbed through substitution, inventories, rerouting, international assistance, technological innovation, or higher prices, but simultaneous crises can turn those independent safety mechanisms into correlated failures and progressively exhaust the resources required for recovery.

Catastrophic models nevertheless underestimate an essential counterforce: adaptation. Markets redirect supply, governments build reserves and alliances, industries redesign products and diversify suppliers, institutions learn, new technologies emerge, and crises themselves create incentives to eliminate vulnerabilities.

The critical variable is therefore not simply whether globalization declines, but whether disruption propagates faster than societies can adapt. If adaptation remains faster, globalization may be reconfigured into more redundant regional and allied networks; if disruption persistently strains adaptive capacity without overwhelming it, the world may settle into a poorer, more heavily armed, less efficient system of competing blocs; only if cascading failures consistently outrun adaptive capacity does genuine systemic collapse become plausible.

This framework ultimately yields something more defensible than a prophecy: a stress model showing how individually manageable failures can become dangerous when they interact, and highlighting highlighting where the resilience of modern civilization is most vulnerable to interacting failures.

⚡ STRATEGIC BRIEF: PENTAGON REVEALS ORBITAL WEAPONS PROGRAM IN DIRECT CHALLENGE TO CHINA AND RUSSIA

👇 Challenge the global narrative. ⤵️ Follow, Reply & 💗 !

**PENTAGON officials have officially acknowledged operating active offensive weapons in Earth's orbit, triggering a secret space-warfare escalation.**

**This unprecedented public disclosure shifts the nature of global deterrence, transforming space from a supportive domain into an active theater of conflict. By confirming the existence of operational orbital systems designed to counter Chinese and Russian space assets, Washington signals a departure from its historical policy of strategic ambiguity in orbit, setting the stage for a highly destabilizing outer-space arms race.**

GEOPOLITICAL IMPLICATIONS

The acknowledgment of operational orbital assets marks the end of decades of undeclared space militarization.

Washington has decided that deterrence requires public exposure rather than classified secrecy in the face of rapid Chinese and Russian developments.

• Over 500 active satellites are estimated to be operated by China, many with potential dual-use kinetic or electronic warfare capabilities.

• Russia has repeatedly tested direct-ascent anti-satellite missiles and inspected US assets using maneuvering "inspector" satellites.

• The United States Space Force budget has expanded rapidly, reflecting the critical priority placed on orbital defense systems.

By making these weapons public, the US seeks to establish a visible threshold of deterrence, signaling that hostile actions in orbit will meet immediate, active kinetic or non-kinetic responses.

This shift reflects a growing realization within the Department of Defense that secret weapons do not deter adversaries if they do not know they exist.

The strategic calculus has shifted from maintaining a secret operational advantage to signaling a credible retaliatory capability to prevent a preemptive orbital strike.

This disclosure also serves as a warning to commercial space operators, who must now prepare for their infrastructure to become active targets in a conflict.

The integration of commercial constellations like Starlink into military communication networks has blurred the line between civilian and military targets, forcing a revision of orbital rules of engagement.

This disclosure forces both Beijing and Moscow to reassess their escalatory calculations regarding critical space infrastructure.

For years, the asymmetric advantage in space belonged to the United States due to its massive reliance on GPS, communications, and surveillance constellations.

China and Russia developed counter-space capabilities specifically to target this perceived vulnerability during a terrestrial conflict.

The confirmation of US orbital weapons neutralizes this strategic assumption, demonstrating that Washington can actively defend its systems and destroy adversary assets.

• Analysts estimate that a war in space could disable up to 80 percent of global communication and navigation capabilities within hours.

• The economic impact of such a disruption is projected to exceed trillions of dollars in immediate commercial and supply chain losses.

• Debris from kinetic interceptors could render low Earth orbit unusable for decades, creating a barrier known as the Kessler syndrome.

Adversaries must now operate under the assumption that any kinetic attack on American satellites will result in the immediate destruction of their own orbital infrastructure.

This mutual vulnerability mimics the Cold War doctrine of Mutually Assured Destruction, now transposed to the orbital sphere.

The development of co-orbital weapons, which can shadow enemy satellites and disable them on command, creates an unstable environment where the first strike offers a decisive advantage.

The public admission also accelerates the erosion of international outer space treaties and norms.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits weapons of mass destruction in orbit but leaves a major legal vacuum regarding conventional kinetic or directed-energy weapons.

European and Asian allies now face intense pressure to align with the US space security doctrine or risk losing access to integrated orbital defense networks.

This development solidifies a permanent bifurcation of outer space into competing allied blocs, mirroring terrestrial geopolitical alignments on Earth.

• The global space economy is projected to reach 1.8 trillion dollars by 2035, driven largely by military and dual-use defense contracts.

• Over 80 nations now operate or have direct stakes in orbital assets, making the weaponization of this domain a truly global threat.

• Private defense contractors are receiving record funding to develop jam-resistant military communications and satellite replenishment capabilities.

As non-aligned nations are forced to choose between US-led and Sino-Russian space architectures, international space cooperation, such as joint scientific missions, will cease.

The militarization of orbit turns what was once a shared scientific frontier into a highly contested arena of raw geopolitical competition.

This dynamic will trigger an uncoordinated rush to secure orbit-ground communications links, deep-space tracking stations, and exclusive launch facilities.

SYSTEMIC IMPACT

In the long term, this development fundamentally alters global hegemony by cementing orbit as the ultimate high ground of modern warfare.

Strategic dominance is no longer defined solely by terrestrial or naval projection, but by the capacity to control and deny access to the orbital commons.

As the military-industrial complexes of the US, China, and Russia redirect funding toward offensive space technologies, the threshold for conflict decreases.

The weaponization of orbit guarantees that any future major great-power clash will immediately expand into a multi-domain confrontation with catastrophic consequences.

This paradigm shift will render traditional terrestrial defense strategies obsolete, as control over land, sea, and air becomes entirely dependent on maintaining dominance over the orbital layer.

Ultimately, the nation that establishes undisputed control over low Earth orbit will dictate the terms of geopolitical and economic activity on the surface below.

text:
The Atlanta History Files...A group for history and great memories
Lisa Land Cooper - Author and Historian ·
 ·
This colorful postcard shows one of Atlanta’s great landmarks of the 1920s: the Atlanta Biltmore Hotel on West Peachtree Street. Look closely at the roof and you’ll notice something that made the Biltmore especially recognizable — the enormous radio towers stretching above the building.
The Biltmore opened on April 19, 1924, at a reported cost of about $6 million. Local financier William Candler, son of Coca-Cola founder Asa Candler, was a major force behind the project, working with the Bowman-Biltmore hotel organization. The New York architectural firm Schultze & Weaver designed the complex, which included an 11-story hotel and an adjoining 10-story apartment building.
When it opened, the Biltmore was intended to announce that Atlanta had entered a new era. It offered elegant ballrooms, restaurants, luxury accommodations and what the Atlanta History Center/Midtown Alliance historical marker identifies as Atlanta’s first indoor swimming pool. Even the hotel’s opening-night festivities were broadcast nationally by radio.
And radio soon became one of the Biltmore’s most interesting Atlanta connections.
In 1925, WSB moved its studios into the hotel’s upper floor. For several years, the enormous towers seen in this postcard supported WSB’s transmitting antenna. The station continued broadcasting from studios at the Biltmore for roughly three decades, even after the actual transmitter moved elsewhere. Georgia State University’s broadcasting collection preserves a photograph identifying the span between the towers as 312 feet, 6 inches. The towers themselves survived and remain one of the building’s most distinctive features.
For decades, the Biltmore was one of Atlanta’s social centers. Its ballrooms hosted dances, debutante parties, civic dinners and other major events, while its guest list included entertainers, politicians and visiting dignitaries. Franklin D. Roosevelt and actress Bette Davis were among the prominent names associated with the hotel.
The Biltmore changed with Atlanta. Sheraton purchased it in 1967 and operated it for years as the Sheraton-Biltmore. The original Atlanta Biltmore name later returned, but the hotel finally closed in 1982. For years the grand building sat largely unused, and its future was uncertain.
Fortunately, it survived.
A major redevelopment in the late 1990s converted the former hotel floors into office space while restoring surviving historic public rooms, including the ballrooms. The adjoining former apartment building became residences. In 2016, the Georgia Tech Foundation purchased the main Biltmore property, which now forms part of the Technology Square area.
So, unlike many grand Atlanta hotels of its era, the Biltmore is still with us at 817 West Peachtree Street.
And those peculiar towers in the postcard are more than architectural decoration. They are reminders of a time when hotel guests could dance downstairs while, high above them, WSB was helping introduce Atlanta — quite literally — to the airwaves.

text:
HEROES & HEROINES OF TROY 
PART XIV

PARIS | ΠΑΡΙΣ — ἈΛΕΞΑΝΔΡΟΣ

Before the armies.

Before the ships.

Before ten years of war…

There was a choice.

Paris was a prince of Troy, son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba and brother of Hector.

Greek tradition tells that Paris was chosen to judge a contest between three goddesses:

Hera. Athena. Aphrodite.

Each offered him something.

Hera offered power.

Athena offered martial glory and wisdom.

Aphrodite offered him the love of the most beautiful woman in the world:

Helen of Sparta.

Paris chose Aphrodite.

And the famous Judgment of Paris became one of the legendary events leading toward the Trojan War.

But Homer gives us a more complicated Paris.

He can be beautiful and charismatic, yet Hector rebukes him for failing to bear the consequences of what he helped begin.

Paris nevertheless fights.

In the Iliad, he wounds several Achaean warriors with his bow.

And later Greek tradition gives him one of the most consequential shots in mythology:

the arrow that kills Achilles, aided by Apollo.

Paris was never Troy’s Hector.

He was something different.

A prince whose choice became larger than himself.

One judgment.
One woman.
A thousand ships.
And a city destined to burn.

Homer, Iliad
The Judgment of Paris — wider Greek mythic tradition

Before Hollywood, there was Homer.

Allan E. Parker

Tue, Sep 15 at 2:22 PM

Thank you to all of you who supported our brief writing, the travel, and prayer for the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals Oral Argument on September 9, at 9:00 a.m.!

As our previous emails reported, The Justice Foundation filed two briefs on behalf of 2,796 Women Hurt By Abortion, the National Association of Christian Lawmakers and National Institute for Family and Life Advocates. Allan Parker presented at The Way of Life Conference in St. Paul, which was attended by the Archbishop of St. Paul, Minnesota, and the President of the Missouri Lutheran Synod, as well as numerous other religious organizations.

The Justice Foundation

THE LEGACY REBRAND IS WILD 🦖🇨🇦
Shams Charania reporting that Kawhi Leonard rejected long-term extension offers from Detroit and Minnesota to force his way back to the Toronto Raptors is top-tier selective nostalgia. Man spent 2019 walking away from a championship team to play in LA, and now that the Clippers experiment has spiraled into cap circumvention chaos, he’s pitching Canada as a "legacy play." Toronto fans might get a second ring out of it, but let’s stop acting like this wasn’t his absolute safety net.
